amit@amitisinvesting
09:22 SGTInvesting
$PLTR

Palantir, once again, puts up one of the best quarters that the market has ever seen.

Being able to grow revenues 96% while having 62% adjusted operating income margins is unheard of. There is no other software company that is even close to putting up these types of results.

US commercial revenue officially passed US government revenue for the first time. I remember in 2022, the bear case was centered around the company being too reliant on the USG. If anything, that was the bull case because that gave them the time to figure out how to scale US commercial and now we have a company doing 29% growth QoQ, which would be amazing YoY for most companies as Dr. Karp said, but also scaling that YoY growth at 148% for US commercial.

It is unprecedented.

So, why? Why is it happening?

Well, it seems like Sovereignty is a very, very big deal.

“The Sovereign AI movement is imposing the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots that I have witnessed in 30 years of business. Every institution—government and commercial—is rapidly being forced, voluntarily or not, into one of these two categories,” said Alex Karp.

Having been to multiple AIPCons and Institutional Sovereignty bootcamps this year, I can say that this is very real. When you talk to customers, you realize that they want much, much more than just plugging their enterprise into an LLM. They actually want FDEs, they want the grunt work of figuring out how to build custom workflows, they want the post training and fine tuning of open models...they want outcomes. The reason Palantir is growing this fast and continuing to show so much operating leverage is because they are delivering outcomes. That's why this is working.

The company is doing this with 1090 customers. Most enterprise software companies at this scale have well over 100K customers. I mean, once again, this is unprecedented. The merger combines Marvell's expertise in custom AI chips, switching, and electrical interconnects with Lumentum's leadership in lasers, optical transceivers, and optical circuit switching, positioning the combined business to address an estimated $550B total addressable market.

Under the proposed partnership, Bloom would provide its on-site power generation systems, while CRC's Carbon TerraVault would handle CO2 transportation and permanent underground storage. The projects, being evaluated across Central and Northern California, could supply electricity to AI data centers, utilities, and industrial customers, with the companies estimating that up to 3 million metric tons of CO2 annually could be available for capture and storage.

11. AST SpaceMobile $ASTS and AT&T $T announced the first successful handoff of an active cellular connection between a terrestrial network and a satellite network using an unmodified smartphone, marking a significant milestone for direct-to-device satellite connectivity. The test successfully transferred an active connection between AT&T's ground-based cellular infrastructure and AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird satellites, leveraging networking technology from Ericsson $ERIC and Nokia $NOK. The achievement demonstrates progress toward enabling ordinary smartphones to transition between traditional cell towers and satellite coverage without requiring specialized hardware. AT&T said the next step will involve real-world beta testing ahead of a potential commercial rollout, bringing AST SpaceMobile closer to delivering satellite-based cellular coverage in areas where conventional networks are unavailable.

12. Piper Sandler believes a potential SpaceX $SPCX and Tesla $TSLA merger proposal is now more likely than not, as both companies have reportedly established independent special committees to evaluate a possible combination. The firm expects Elon Musk to retain more than 70% voting control of the combined entity under most potential transaction structures, allowing him to maintain significant influence over the businesses. A merger could bring together Tesla's electric vehicles, autonomous driving, robotics, and energy infrastructure with SpaceX's satellite connectivity, launch operations, and AI computing capabilities, potentially creating one of the world's most vertically integrated technology companies.

What's happening now in the stock market is more than just a "correction in tech stocks."

Sure, AI CapEx concerns are legitimate and investors will always care about profitability.

But, there's more beneath the surface here.

The reality is that the market is pricing-in a major shift in the political landscape of the US.

Over the last 12 months, market expectations for a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections have tripled.

Over the last 45 days alone, these expectations are up +30 percentage points.

As it stands, markets themselves now see a near-80% chance of a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections.

President Trump has already vowed to become "Mr. Veto" if this in fact does happen.

This is post is not political, it's objective. A change in the political landscape always comes with uncertainty; markets hate uncertainty.

Objectively, the market is in the process of pricing-in two years of political gridlock.

Could this change? Of course. But markets price-in the most probable outcome, and the odds now overwhelmingly favor the aforementioned scenario.

Tomorrow sets the stage for the next two years.

$LITE & $MRVL Scenario Analysis & Explanations:

TLDR: Lumentum brings ~a third of the combined profit to the Marvell deal and gets ~a third of the company. Why would a business more than doubling its revenue accept that? There's no real premium on what it brings!!!! 🚨

* Each cell compares Lumentum holders' share of the combined company's profit vs. what they'd have kept if Lumentum stayed independent.
** Red cells = Lumentum holders are worse off in the deal. Green = better off.
*** n/m = Lumentum makes a loss on its own, so a % comparison isn't meaningful.

Explanations:
- If Lumentum keeps growing, shareholders lose in every column: −12.5% if Marvell hits its $20B FY28 outlook, −33% if Marvell stalls, −43% in a downturn.
- If Lumentum just holds today's level, holders only win if Marvell hits $20B (+17%).
- If Lumentum's margins fall back to last year's 15%, the deal protects them: +46% to +188%.

This kind of shape is normal...every all-stock deal looks like this. You swap 100% of your company for a fixed slice of a bigger one, so you give away some upside if your company outperforms and get cushioned if it doesn't. Again, normal.

-> What's NOT normal is where *today* sits on the grid!!!! 🚨

Usually the target is paid a premium on top of what it brings. That shifts the whole grid green, so holders still win if their company keeps performing.

Here, Lumentum holders get ~33%, and Lumentum already earns ~31% of the combined profit (~35% on next quarter's guidance).

There's no real premium. The breakeven sits right at today!!!!! 🚨🚨🚨

For comparison, here's how the grid changes if they'd got a 40% stake:
- Keeps growing + Marvell hits outlook: −12.5% becomes +6%.
- Holds today's level + Marvell stays put: −14% becomes +4%.

-> Why so little?

1. The $1,132 / 23.9% premium announced today was over Lumentum's share price, which already valued Lumentum more cheaply than Marvell for the profit it makes.
2. So the premium only got holders to their fair share, not above it.
3. And it's paid in Marvell stock at a fixed ratio: with Marvell down ~30% since the leak last week, it's now worth ~$800, below Lumentum's pre-leak price.

-> Feels like the trend is against them too.

1. Lumentum's share of the combined profit has gone from a loss in mid-2024 to 9%, 27%, 31%, and ~35% next quarter.
2. The 33% is fixed, so everything above it goes to Marvell holders.
3. Even if Marvell delivers, Lumentum only needs ~26% more profit than today's run-rate to cross into the red, and its own guidance shows ~36% growth in a single quarter.

IMO Lumentum management thinks current margins are unsustainable and that CPO hands power to companies like Marvell.

If they're wrong, they sold the fastest-growing part of the combined company for roughly what it contributes... while its share was still rising......!!!!!!

[Non-GAAP operating profit from company filings and guidance. Scenarios use Marvell's own FY28 outlook]

Since 1980, the S&P 500 has rallied +2.1% on average in November, making it the strongest month of the year.

Over this period, positive returns occurred 74% of the time, the best hit rate of any month.

Furthermore, the S&P 500 has gained +1.6% on average in November since 1964, with positive returns occurring 69% of the time.

The highest November return during this period was +10.8%, recorded in 2020.

History points to a strong month ahead.

Some thoughts on talking to management teams, after today's chat with $NAUT management

1/ I get to know management teams very well primarily by looking at key variables of a business and by observing how management teams act in challenging times. Ultimately, I look for an ability to focus on long term value creation and make it happen
2/ I typically synthesise this into wether a business has an abnormally high ability to solve a growing volume of acute customer pains while keeping costs in check, thus increasing the top line exponentially and bringing much of that down to the bottom line: fcf/share
3/ I get to know management teams so well over the long term that I can fully delegate anything on management teams that have been in my portfolio for, in some cases, more than 10 years
4/ I have never talked to a management team before or after having performed this kind of analysis, let alone right at the start of my shareholder journey and in such an early stage operation. It's almost like in hearing the tone, its slight variations, the shift from the specific to the abstract and back, I'm able to track KPIs back to specific part of each manager's personality
5/ My conclusion from today's podcast is that $NAUT management can solve a growing volume of acute customer pains in a way that's increasingly harder to replicate, while keeping costs in check, and that extrapolated over a decade the odds of this yielding a highly valuable and hard to replicate new data layer are appealing enough to occupy a spot in my portfolio. I believe revenue will trend up and that $NAUT will do more with less over time

Nasdaq $QQQ has seen significant distribution lately, and we're approaching correction territory (-10% from the highs). After Friday's gap down, $QQQ is now facing rejection near Friday's highs. There's a good chance we test the 200-day SMA, and that's where we'll need to see whether buyers step in. If that level fails, the next major support is around the double-bottom area in the $660s.

$SMH is barely holding its 200-day SMA, while many semiconductor leaders are already trading well below theirs. I'd be cautious about picking long ideas in the semiconductor sector right now. It's better to wait for these names to complete their Stage 4 declines and start building Stage 1 bases, which could mean sideways price action for weeks or even months.

Midterms are tomorrow, and I think some of the negative catalysts may already be priced in, which could explain why $QQQ is approaching correction territory. At the same time, I really don't like seeing earnings-related gap-downs in major names like $GOOGL and $INTC. Ideally, if the market is going to establish a new uptrend and produce the next generation of leaders, here's what we want to see:

- A Follow-Through Day (FTD) on the major indexes.
- Powerful earnings gap-up candles (PEGs) following strong earnings reports.
- More Stage 1 bases forming with signs of institutional accumulation.
- More stocks making new 52-week highs and fewer stocks making new lows.

So far, we're not seeing enough of these signals to suggest a sustainable new uptrend.

Until then, focus on building your watchlist, identifying stocks showing relative strength, and studying which sectors are holding up better than the broader market.

One of the most expensive habits in the stock market is feeling the need to participate in every move.

You see a stock rally 10-15% without you, and suddenly your entire framework goes out the window. You start chasing stocks in downtrends, ignoring risk, and convincing yourself that this time is different.

That's FOMO, and it can do more damage to your portfolio than a bad earnings report.

You can spend years studying technical analysis, fundamental analysis, CANSLIM, and Stage Analysis. You can identify great companies, understand their financials, and recognize the strongest trends.

But none of that matters much if you can't control your emotions when the market starts moving against your expectations.

The market doesn't reward you simply for knowing more than everyone else. Knowledge is important, but the ability to execute your process consistently is what makes the difference over time.

Sometimes the best decision is buying a stock. Sometimes it's selling a stock. And sometimes it's doing absolutely nothing, even when everyone around you seems to be making money.

Missing a rally won't destroy your portfolio. Repeatedly abandoning your discipline to chase rallies eventually can.

There will always be another stock, another breakout, and another opportunity.

The goal isn't to participate in every move. It's to make sure the decisions you make are worth the risks you're accepting.

Patience and discipline are just as important as technicals and fundamentals.

Paradis@ParadisLabs
22:06 SGTInvesting
$LITE shareholders should be annoyed...

The 23.9% premium in the $MRVL deal is real on paper, but in dollars it's gone.

1. 4.5 $MRVL per $LITE = $1,132/share on 28 Oct = 23.9% above Lumentum's undisturbed $914.

This is the 23.9% premium reported today.

2. Marvell has since fallen ~22% to $196.40 (Friday close).

So 4.5 shares = ~$884 = 3.3% below Lumentum’s undisturbed price of $914.

3. The deal's $102.5B equity value is now ~$80B.

4. Lumentum fell ~8% in the same selloff to the ~$840s.

5. So even vs where Lumentum actually trades, the premium has shrunk from 23.9% to ~5%.

I think Marvell needs to get back above ~$203 for Lumentum shareholders to see any premiums over the undisturbed price.

It's essentially a premium paid in a currency (stock) that’s fallen 22%.

Welcome any pushback on my napkin math calcs. By no means a comprehensive model.

Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal:

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable.

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027.

If I had to guess:

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now.

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use.

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains.

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company.

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year.

So M&A premiums likely went up.

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expansion + tiny MC.

$JBL also probably wants to vertically integrate down the road too so $SIVE is also an acquisition target for their 1.6T program.

$AMD was looking for ELSFP + CW capacity given Nvidia bottlenecks, so I'm sure they've looked at $AAOI.

can go on and on about other ASIC players (like in Taiwan) that likely are looking at vertical integration too.

Since multiple players use a small subset of laser suppliers, if competitors just go ahead and buys them...

There's a lot pressure to M&A for their own supply chain defensibility.

TLDR: Independent laser suppliers should capture a material strategic revaluation since $MRVL + $LITE, sets a new precedent + implications.

We'll see what happens.

$MRVL to acquire $LITE in an all-stock transaction.

- Implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum.

- Lumentum stockholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each share of Lumentum common stock.

- This represents ~$1,132 per share of Lumentum common stock and a premium of approximately 23.9% based on each company’s price as of October 28, 2026.

- Marvell stockholders will own ~67% of the combined company. Lumentum stockholders will own ~33%.

- Matt Murphy to remain as CEO of the combined company.

- Transaction expected to close in H1 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

We've finally made it to November... holy crap October was brutal.

Per Morgan Stanley data, the recent hedge fund de-grossing was the highest in the past 10 years.

Exceeding the:
- 2016 Chinese stock market crash
- 2018 Volmageddon
- March 2020 COVID crash
- 2021 Archegos collapse / Evergrande crisis
- 2022 bear market

Goldman's prime brokerage desk reported on the 26th that it had also seen ~$20B of selling over 2 weeks vs. $23 billion during July's entire unwind.

From $HOOD short interest data, from Sept -> Oct short float also increased from:

$AAOI: 12.5% -> 19.84%+
$AEVA: 11% -> 25.64%+
$CBRS: 12.25% -> 20.12%+
$AEHR: 14.33% -> 17.93%+
$TSEM: 2.15% -> 4.73%+
$CIFR: 19.94% -> 25.39%+
$LWLG: 15.24% ->19.12%+
$OKLO: 17.72% ->22.93%+
$CRWV: 17.91% ->26.58%+

Substantial deleveraging coinciding with surging short interest, kinda looks like a July setup after Midterms?

The recent rotation also kinda pushed names like $CRWD and cybersecurity to bubble valuations into hundreds of fwd P/E...

Earnings on many AI capex + bottlenecks (not all like $INTC) looked strong:

eg. $AXTI guided annualized Q4 = 23.7x P/E now, not including potential InP substrate hikes + capacity expansion that can compress it to single digits.

- $SKHY (~$59B operating profit) casually making more than trillion dollar companies like Amazon ($28.1B operating profit), backed with 5Y LTAs.

- No signs of $MSFT / $AMZN materially cutting capex, while $SPCX secures $40B more for GPU procurement.

Slightly painful, but I think the AI capex trade (specifically photonics/memory) is a generational opportunity, with extreme volatility in between.

Weekly Portfolio Update | November 1st 📊
Well, this was a pretty brutal week for my portfolio...

A few of my largest holdings got absolutely crushed, but my long-term conviction hasn't changed.

What Happened This Week:

$NOW was easily the biggest disappointment from a stock price perspective, falling roughly 34% this week.

I actually liked a lot of what I saw in the earnings report. The business continues growing, AI adoption is expanding, and the valuation has become significantly more attractive.

$AMZN also took a hit following earnings, despite AWS delivering some incredible numbers. The market is concerned about Amazon's massive capital spending, but I'm optimistic about the long-term returns those investments could generate.

$AMD was another painful one, with disappointing commentary from $INTC adding pressure to the stock.

AMD reports next week, and I'm excited to see what management has to say.

What I Bought:

$SOFI at $14.54

$BN at $38.29
Both remain high-conviction investments for me, and I'm happy continuing to accumulate shares when opportunities present themselves.

What I Sold:

Nothing.

Despite the volatility, I didn't sell a single share this week.

My Game Plan Going Forward:

I'm continuing to prioritize rebuilding my cash position, but I'm absolutely willing to take advantage of opportunities when they present themselves.

I'm happy with my current $NOW position, but if shares fall to $100 or below again, I'll gladly add more.

I'm also watching $BN around $35 and continuing to look for opportunities in $NFLX, $UBER, $AMZN, and $SOFI.

For now, I'm comfortable with my other positions and have no plans to make any major changes.

Obviously, watching your portfolio take a beating isn't fun. But I'm investing in where I believe these businesses will be five or ten years from now.

A rough week doesn't change that.

How did everyone else's portfolio hold up this week?

Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
hackertube.org

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

George from 🕹prodmgmt.world@nurijanian
06:36 SGT quoteTech
super interesting that Patrick is doing this

(there are also a bunch of startups now that let end users modify existing software)

managing this at scale may be a non-issue due to the already artisanal nature of vibe coded tools, i.e. none might reach the scale that’s hard to manage (with ever improving agents) - besides, how much modification do you really need?

but if some tool became really popular yet required a lot of modifications/continuous mods, you could imagine a few movements:

- extracting the core engine and enabling mods in a marketplace
- some sort of UX arbiter agent that resolves the conflicting features all the time
- permanent forking (with a license fee)

I personally feel like the startups in this space fight too many headwinds: you have to educate the market about your product, while many SaaS are disintermediated by AI at the core, so you’re selling into a dying market, selling panadol to a terminally ill patient

perhaps a better version of this is describing the thing you’re trying to do and getting the agent to cut the gordian knot and solve it without UI or new features.
Patrick Collison @patrickc · 1 Nov 2026, 05:02 SGT
I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

BREAKING: The US personal savings rate fell -0.2 percentage points in September, to 4.2%, its lowest level since October 2022.

Since January 2024, this metric has declined -3.4 percentage points.

The personal savings rate is now well below the 5-year pre-pandemic average of 6.2%.

This comes as personal income grew +4.1% YoY in September, its 2nd-lowest growth rate since April 2022.

At the same time, personal consumption expenditures rose +6.3% YoY, the 2nd-highest YoY growth since December 2024.

In other words, consumer spending continues to outpace income growth, putting further pressure on household savings and increasing household reliance on borrowing.

Elevated inflation and record prices are putting further pressure on consumer savings.

US corporate debt issuance is skyrocketing:

US investment-grade corporate bond sales are expected to rise +$37 billion YoY in November, or +27%, to $175 billion, the highest for any November on record.

This would mark a +$76 billion, or +77%, increase from November 2024 level.

To put this into perspective, the 5-year average before 2025 was $104 billion.

By comparison, US investment-grade bond issuance stood at ~$100 billion in October.

As a result, US investment-grade bond sales have risen to a record $1.76 trillion YTD, already surpassing the full-year 2025 total of $1.75 trillion.

Meanwhile, over $300 billion in AI-related corporate bonds have been issued in global investment-grade markets so far in 2026, almost 3 times the total for all of 2025.

AI spending is fueling an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing.
